question.knowledge_point: Solving an Inequality When the Base of the Exponential is Greater Than One
question.worked_solution:
Isolating the exponential term, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}2{e}^{x-2}+1 & <3 \\ 2{e}^{x-2} & <2 \\ {e}^{x-2} & <1.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x-2}) & <\operatorname{ln}⁡1 \\ x-2 & <0 \\ x & <2.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Solving an Inequality When the Base of the Exponential is Between Zero and One
question.worked_solution:
Isolating the exponential term, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}{(0.84)}^{x+5}-20 & >0 \\ {(0.84)}^{x+5} & >20.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡[(0.84)^{x+5}] & >\operatorname{ln}⁡(20) \\ (x+5)\operatorname{ln}⁡(0.84) & >\operatorname{ln}⁡(20)\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, note that $\operatorname{ln}⁡(0.84)$ is a negative quantity, so when we divide both sides by it, we need to flip the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+5 & <\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(20)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(0.84)} \\ x & <\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(20)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(0.84)}-5\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Solving an Inequality When the Base of the Exponential is Between Zero and One
question.worked_solution:
Isolating the exponential term, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}5\cdot {(\frac{4}{9})}^{x} & <25 \\ {(\frac{4}{9})}^{x} & <5.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡[{(\frac{4}{9})}^{x}] & <\operatorname{ln}⁡5 \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{4}{9}) & <\operatorname{ln}⁡5 \\ x(\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\operatorname{ln}⁡9) & <\operatorname{ln}⁡5.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, note that $\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\operatorname{ln}⁡9$ is a negative quantity, so when we divide both sides by it, we need to flip the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & >\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\operatorname{ln}⁡9}\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Solving an Inequality When the Exponential is Compared to Zero or a Negative Number
question.worked_solution:
Isolating the exponential term, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(0.72)^{3x-7}+2 & \le -4 \\ \frac{1}{2}(0.72)^{3x-7} & \le -6 \\ (0.72)^{3x-7} & \le -12.\end{aligned}
$$

Because a power of a positive number is always greater than $0,$ we must have

$$
(0.72)^{3x-7}>0
$$

for all values of $x.$

Therefore, the inequality $(0.72)^{3x-7}\le -12$ has no solutions.

question.knowledge_point: Solving an Inequality When the Exponential is Compared to Zero or a Negative Number
question.worked_solution:
Isolating the exponential term, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5}\cdot {3}^{1-5x}+6 & >0 \\ \frac{3}{5}\cdot {3}^{1-5x} & >-6 \\ {3}^{1-5x} & >-10.\end{aligned}
$$

Because a power of a positive number is always greater than $0,$ we must have

$$
{3}^{1-5x}>0
$$

for all values of $x.$

Therefore, the inequality ${3}^{1-5x}>-10$ is satisfied for all real values of $x.$

question.knowledge_point: Solving an Inequality with Exponential Functions on Both Sides
question.worked_solution:
Taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{x-1} & <{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2-x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({5}^{x-1}) & <\operatorname{ln}⁡[{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2-x}] \\ (x-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡5 & <(2-x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2}) \\ (x-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡5 & <(2-x)(\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\ (x-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡5 & <(2-x)(0-\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\ (x-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡5 & <(x-2)\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡5-\operatorname{ln}⁡5 & <x\operatorname{ln}⁡2-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡5-x\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & <\operatorname{ln}⁡5-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ x(\operatorname{ln}⁡5-\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & <\operatorname{ln}⁡5-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ x & <\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡5-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.worked_solution:
Taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{4}^{1-2x} & \le 3\cdot {5}^{2-3x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({4}^{1-2x}) & \le \operatorname{ln}⁡(3\cdot {5}^{2-3x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({4}^{1-2x}) & \le \operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+\operatorname{ln}⁡({5}^{2-3x}) \\ (1-2x)\operatorname{ln}⁡4 & \le \operatorname{ln}⁡3+(2-3x)\operatorname{ln}⁡5 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡4-2x\operatorname{ln}⁡4 & \le \operatorname{ln}⁡3+2\operatorname{ln}⁡5-3x\operatorname{ln}⁡5 \\ 3x\operatorname{ln}⁡5-2x\operatorname{ln}⁡4 & \le \operatorname{ln}⁡3+2\operatorname{ln}⁡5-\operatorname{ln}⁡4 \\ x(3\operatorname{ln}⁡5-2\operatorname{ln}⁡4) & \le \operatorname{ln}⁡3+2\operatorname{ln}⁡5-\operatorname{ln}⁡4 \\ x & \le \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡3+2\operatorname{ln}⁡5-\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡5-2\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\end{aligned}
$$
